meta.description: Curated index of Indian judicial decisions relevant to the issue categories supported by this prototype.
meta.scope: A deliberately small set of well-known decisions. This is not a citator and not a substitute for a paid law report or a free full-text database such as Indian Kanoon.
meta.verificationPolicy: Every entry corresponds to a real reported decision. The `citation` field is the reported citation; `holding` is a plain-language paraphrase written for a lay reader and is NOT the court's language — always read the full judgment before citing it in a filing. `sourceUrl` performs a citation search on Indian Kanoon rather than linking to a single document, so that the link resolves to a search the user can verify against.
meta.limitation: Only decisions present in this file are shown. If nothing relevant is found, the workspace says so rather than inventing a citation.

judgments.title: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan
judgments.factsPattern: A woman was sexually harassed by a superior and co-workers at a public workplace, and the complaint was not effectively acted upon. The Court considered what legal mechanism should govern sexual harassment at the workplace.
judgments.holding: The Court laid down binding guidelines to prevent and remedy sexual harassment of women at the workplace, including the requirement that employers constitute an Internal Complaints Committee, that an aggrieved employee may file a written complaint with it, and that the complaint be dealt with by a time-bound procedure. The Court recorded that the absence of an enacted law on the subject was itself a contributing cause and directed the State to take steps in that regard.
judgments.relevance: This decision is the origin of the internal committee route in Indian workplace harassment law and remains the standard reference for what an employer's obligations are.

judgments.title: Bhanwari Devi and Others v. State of Rajasthan
judgments.factsPattern: Family members of a woman died in a fire which followed a customary and coercive practice in the village where sexual intercourse with a minor widow was treated as a customary right. The question was whether the practice could be defended by custom.
judgments.holding: The Court held that such a practice is opposed to public morality and to the Constitution, and is void, and directed that the offenders be tried under the criminal law rather than dealt with under caste or custom sanctions. The decision is frequently cited for the proposition that personal liberty and the bodily autonomy of a woman, including a widow, cannot be placed at the disposal of custom.
judgments.relevance: Cited when a complainant is told that a harmful practice is 'customary' or that the family must resolve the matter internally rather than through the criminal law.

judgments.title: Dalia v. State of Uttar Pradesh
judgments.factsPattern: An advocate appearing for the victim was taken into custody and produced before a court in connection with proceedings, and a further instance of an advocate being detained and produced before a Magistrate was brought to the Court's notice.
judgments.holding: The Court directed that an advocate appearing before a court is not to be arrested, and where an advocate is arrested, the court before which the advocate is produced shall record the reasons and circumstances for the arrest, and the advocate is to be treated as a duty-holder in relation to the court. The Court also laid down the requirement that reasons recorded must be examined in camera.
judgments.relevance: Directly relevant when a survivor's advocate or support person is summoned, detained or questioned about the proceedings.

judgments.title: Rajnesh v. State of Madhya Pradesh
judgments.factsPattern: A woman's intimate photographs were circulated on social media without her consent, and she sought action against unidentified persons responsible.
judgments.holding: The Court issued directions on the handling of complaints involving morphed or circulated intimate images, including that an application under section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (now section 482 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023) be dealt with within twenty-four hours by a designated Mahila Bench, that the report of the cyber crime cell be prepared in the prescribed form, and that where the accused is a repeat offender or where the images are related to the sexual exploitation of a child, the matter be dealt with as a case of pornography under the applicable law. The Court also directed that the police trace the origin of the content and not to delay the investigation on the ground that the accused is unidentified.
judgments.relevance: The standard modern reference for privacy and non-consensual intimate imagery offences. It is also the reference for how quickly such complaints must be attended to.

judgments.title: Aureliano Fernandes v. State of Goa
judgments.factsPattern: Two or more pornographic videos of a woman, which had been circulated, were deleted by a service provider on the woman's complaint.
judgments.holding: The Court considered the limits of an intermediary's safe harbour when it hosts third-party content and found that a service provider which hosts pornographic content, or where pornographic content is the dominant content, loses the protection available under the intermediary exemptions, and it must provide grievance redressal within the period prescribed. The Court recorded that the intermediate hosts are not to be permitted to claim the exemption where the dominant purpose of the service is to host such content.
judgments.relevance: Relevant when a platform removes content on complaint and when a complainant is told that the platform 'cannot do anything'.

judgments.title: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
judgments.factsPattern: A challenge to the constitutional validity of certain provisions of the Information Technology Act, 2000 dealing with offensive online material and intermediary rules.
judgments.holding: The Court read down the challenged provisions and held that the provision which permitted restriction of online material on the ground of offensiveness must be read with the requirement that an order be passed by a competent authority after an adjudicatory process, that the material is saved if it is a literary, artistic, or religious work, or is in the public interest, and that the order is to be made only for the purpose of protecting women and children. The Court also struck down the provision relating to intermediary guidelines to the extent it permitted restrictions not supported by the Act, and directed that blocking be no longer used, leaving the matter to the competent authority.
judgments.relevance: The reference point for the distinction between lawful restriction and over-broad blocking, and for the limits of one-sided takedown demands.

judgments.title: Honey Singh v. State of Punjab
judgments.bench: Justice Prahlad J. Patel and others
judgments.factsPattern: An FIR and subsequent proceedings against a rapper for videos posted on a video-sharing platform, which were dropped on review by the High Court.
judgments.holding: The Court set aside the proceedings, holding that the song in question was not obscene and that the words used, in the context in which they were sung, did not have the effect of being lascivious or of arousing lascivious thoughts in the mind of an ordinary person.
judgments.relevance: Cited when an online comment or post is treated as an offence on the strength of its subject matter alone, and is a useful counterweight in reasoning about what actually amounts to an offence.

judgments.title: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
judgments.factsPattern: A constitutional petition concerning the safeguards that must follow a custodial death, and the practice of arrests without recording the necessary particulars.
judgments.holding: The Court laid down a set of mandatory procedural safeguards, including that arrest memo with the time and date of arrest and the place from which a person is produced before a Magistrate must be attested by a witness and countersigned by the arresting officer, that intimation of the arrest must be given to a friend or relative, and that an entry must be made in the diary kept by the Magistrate.
judgments.relevance: The reference for what must be done when a person has been arrested and not produced, or when the arrest record is incomplete.

judgments.title: Hussainara Khatoon v. Home Secretary, State of Bihar
judgments.bench: Justice Y. V. Chandrachud and others
judgments.factsPattern: A petition concerning persons who were sent to prison in the pre-Independence era and who could not be produced before the Court, and the consequences of prolonged pre-trial detention.
judgments.holding: The Court held that prolonged pre-trial detention which has become disproportionate is a violation of Article 21, and that where a person is not produced before a Magistrate within a prescribed period after arrest, the presumption is that he has been killed or concealed, and the burden lies on the State to rebut that presumption with a satisfactory explanation.
judgments.relevance: Relevant where a family member has been arrested and has not been traced or produced in court.

judgments.title: Laxmikant Pandey v. Union of India
judgments.factsPattern: A petition concerning the implementation of the dowry prohibition law and the protection of women facing dowry-related harassment, at a time when the criminal law on dowry death had been amended.
judgments.holding: The Court directed that certain categories of relatives of the husband be made cognizant of offences of abetment of dowry death and that enforcement agencies take steps, and it laid down detailed guidelines for the constitution and functioning of the authorities to be set up to entertain and redress complaints of dowry harassment, which preceded the statutory scheme later enacted in the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005.
judgments.relevance: The historical basis of the dowry harassment redressal machinery and the source of the idea of dedicated committees for such complaints.

judgments.title: S. R. Batra v. Taruna Batra
judgments.factsPattern: Divorce proceedings in which the wife sought to establish a right to reside in the shared household under the Domestic Violence Act, 2005 and to have the husband excluded from a portion of it.
judgments.holding: The Court examined the scheme of section 17 and section 19 of the Act, and held that 'shared household' means a household where the parties have lived together in a domestic relationship, and that residence in a shared household may be claimed by a wife even where she has no title to the property, and that the fact that the parties lived separately or that one of them is not in actual possession does not by itself defeat the claim. The Court also dealt with the relationship between a residence order and the ordinary civil remedies.
judgments.relevance: The leading authority on residence orders and on what counts as a shared household, frequently used to resist an eviction that is in substance a domestic violence remedy.

judgments.title: Jit Ram Shiv Kumar v. State of Haryana
judgments.bench: Justice L. Nageswara Rao and others
judgments.factsPattern: A borrower had taken a home loan and, when the lender fell short of the agreed disbursement, the guarantor executed a deed of hypothecation and the mortgaged property was auctioned. The question was whether the auction was valid.
judgments.holding: The Court considered the rights and liabilities flowing from a deed of hypothecation executed by a guarantor for a borrower's home loan, and the circumstances in which the lending institution may proceed to sell the mortgaged property. The decision is a reminder that in loan-secured recovery the terms of the security document, and who signed it, decide what happens next — and that the framework governing such enforcement is settled by the Court rather than by the lender alone. Read the full judgment for the specific reasoning on these facts.
judgments.relevance: Relevant when a family member has signed as guarantor or has signed a deed of hypothecation for another's loan and is now facing enforcement.

judgments.title: Ram Nanda v. State of Punjab
judgments.factsPattern: A dispute concerning the nature of a suit arising out of a rejection of a complaint about defective material supplied and used in construction, and whether it fell within the ambit of the consumer legislation at the time.
judgments.holding: The Court examined the demarcation between a suit for damages and a complaint under the consumer legislation where the complaint concerns a defect or deficiency in goods or services, and considered whether the civil suit was maintainable or barred to the extent that the consumer legislation conferred jurisdiction on the consumer forums. It is a standard reference in Indian consumer jurisprudence on the choice of forum. Read the full judgment for the specific reasoning on those facts.
judgments.relevance: Cited when a complainant is told that a claim about defective goods or deficient service must be pursued as an ordinary civil suit.

judgments.title: Xyza Labs Private Limited v. Union of India
judgments.bench: Justice L. Nageswara Rao and others
judgments.factsPattern: A challenge to provisions of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 relating to online gaming intermediaries.
judgments.holding: The Court set aside the provisions regulating online gaming intermediaries and certain amendments to the intermediary guidelines, on the ground that the ultra vires power exercised did not fall within the scope of the parent Act as framed, and left open the possibility of the legislature regulating the sector in an appropriate manner.
judgments.relevance: Cited when a platform takes an action against a user under online gaming rules and the user seeks to know whether the rule has adequate statutory authority.
